{{Short description|Any binary relation equal to its composition with itself}}
In mathematics, an '''idempotent binary relation''' is a [[binary relation]] ''R'' on a set ''X'' (a subset of  [[Cartesian product]] ''X''&nbsp;×&nbsp;''X'') for which the [[Relation composition|composition of relations]] ''R''&nbsp;∘&nbsp;''R'' is the same as ''R''.<ref>{{cite tech report| author=Florian Kammüller, J. W. Sanders| title=Idempotent Relation in Isabelle/HOL| year=2004| number=2004-04| pages=27| institution=TU Berlin| url=http://cs.tu-berlin.de/cs/ifb/Ahmed/RoteReihe/2004/TR2004_04.pdf| accessdate=2014-05-10| archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140512224409/http://cs.tu-berlin.de/cs/ifb/Ahmed/RoteReihe/2004/TR2004_04.pdf| archivedate=2014-05-12| url-status=dead}} Here:p.3</ref><ref>{{cite journal| author=Florian Kammüller| title=Mechanical Analysis of Finite Idempotent Relations| year=2011|journal=Fundamenta Informaticae|volume=107|pages=43–65|doi=10.3233/FI-2011-392| url=https://eprints.mdx.ac.uk/6845/1/Kammuller-mechanical_analysis_-WRITTEN_1-11.pdf}}</ref> This notion generalizes that of an [[idempotent function]] to relations.

==Definition==
As a shorthand, the notation ''xRy'' indicates that a pair (''x'',''y'') belongs to a relation ''R''.
The [[Relation composition|composition of relations]] ''R''&nbsp;∘&nbsp;''R'' is the relation ''S''
defined by setting ''xSz'' to be true for a pair of elements ''x'' and ''z'' in ''X'' whenever there exists ''y'' in ''X'' with
''xRy'' and ''yRz'' both true. ''R'' is idempotent if ''R''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''S''.

Equivalently, relation ''R'' is idempotent if and only if the following two properties are true:
*''R'' is a [[transitive relation]], meaning that ''R''&nbsp;∘&nbsp;''R''&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;''R''. Equivalently, in terms of individual elements, for every ''x'', ''y'', and ''z'' for which ''xRy'' and ''yRz'' are both true, ''xRz'' is also true.
*''R''&nbsp;∘&nbsp;''R''&nbsp;⊇&nbsp;''R''. Equivalently, in terms of individual elements, for every ''x'' and ''z'' for which ''xRz'' is true, there exists ''y'' with ''xRy'' and ''yRz'' both true. Some authors call such an ''R'' a [[dense relation]].<ref>[[Gunter Schmidt]] (2011) ''Relational Mathematics'', page 212, [[Cambridge University Press]] {{ISBN|978-0-521-76268-7}}</ref>
Because idempotence incorporates both transitivity and the second property above, it is a stronger property than transitivity.

==Examples==
For example, the relation&nbsp;< on the [[rational number]]s is idempotent. The strict ordering relation is transitive, and whenever two rational numbers ''x'' and ''z'' obey the relation ''x''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''z'' there necessarily exists another rational number ''y'' between them (for instance, their average) with ''x''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''y'' and ''y''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''z''.

In contrast, the same ordering relation&nbsp;<&nbsp;on the [[integer]]s is not idempotent. It is still transitive, but does not obey the second property of an idempotent relation. For instance, 1&nbsp;<&nbsp;2 but there does not exist any other integer ''y'' between 1 and 2.

An [[logical matrix#Logical vectors|outer product of logical vectors]] forms an idempotent relation. Such a relation may be contained in a more complex relation, in which case it is called a '''concept''' in that larger context. The description of relations in terms of their concepts is called [[formal concept analysis]].

==Uses==
Idempotent relations have been used as an example to illustrate the application of Mechanized Formalisation
of mathematics using the interactive theorem prover Isabelle/HOL. Besides checking the mathematical properties of finite idempotent relations, an algorithm for counting the number of idempotent relations has been derived in Isabelle/HOL.<ref>{{cite journal| author=Florian Kammüller| title=Number of idempotent relations on n labeled elements|year=2006|journal=The On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences|number=A12137|url=https://oeis.org/search?q=11%2C123%2C2360&sort=&language=english&go=Search}}</ref><ref>{{cite tech report| author=Florian Kammüller| title=Counting Idempotent Relations| year=2008| number=2008-15| pages=27| institution=TU Berlin| url=http://www.eecs.tu-berlin.de/fileadmin/f4/TechReports/2008/2008-15.pdf}}</ref>

Idempotent relations defined on [[Limit point compact|weakly countably compact spaces]] have also been shown to satisfy "condition Γ": that is, every nontrivial idempotent relation on such a space contains points <math>\langle x,x\rangle, \langle x,y\rangle,\langle y,y\rangle</math> for some <math>x,y</math>. This is used to show that certain [[subspace topology|subspaces]] of an uncountable [[product topology|product]] of spaces, known as Mahavier products, cannot be [[Metric space|metrizable]] when defined by a nontrivial idempotent relation.<ref>
